meta.title: Who really said "A society gets all the criminals it deserves"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Emma Goldman. The line is Alexandre Lacassagne's, put into English by Havelock Ellis in 1890; Goldman quoted Ellis in her 1910 essay on prisons.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A society gets all the criminals it deserves'?
meta.ogDescription: Goldman quoted it in 1910 — inside quotation marks. The line belongs to French criminologist Alexandre Lacassagne, via Havelock Ellis (1890).

answer.label: Not Emma Goldman — actually Alexandre Lacassagne
answer.sourceLine: The sentence belongs to the French criminologist Alexandre Lacassagne. Havelock Ellis put it into English in The Criminal (1890) — “every society has the criminals that it deserves” — and Emma Goldman quoted Ellis, inside quotation marks and with a footnote, in her 1910 essay “Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure.” The quotation marks fell off; her name stayed on. The popular wording — “gets all the criminals” — matches neither Ellis nor Goldman.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: 1890 — Walter Scott, London; Scribner & Welford, New York
Ellis’s English wording, quoting Lacassagne — he gives no French text and no translator note

source.excerpt: Society prepares crimes, as Quetelet said; the criminal is the instrument that executes them. “The social environment,” Lacassagne has well said, “is the cultivation medium of criminality; the criminal is the microbe, an element which only becomes important when it finds the medium which causes it to ferment: every society has the criminals that it deserves.”
trail: 1890 — into English. Havelock Ellis, in chapter I of The Criminal ↗, writes that “Lacassagne has well said” the social environment is the cultivation medium of criminality — closing with “every society has the criminals that it deserves.”

1910 — Goldman quotes Ellis. In “Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure,” collected in Anarchism and Other Essays ↗, she names Ellis, names Lacassagne, puts the sentence in quotation marks and footnotes it “THE CRIMINAL.” The essay was reprinted in the 1917 third revised edition.

The French wording. Lacassagne’s biography ↗ records the aphorism in his own language — « la justice flétrit, la prison corrompt et la société a les criminels qu’elle mérite » — but dates it to his 1913 restatement of the thesis (Archives d’anthropologie criminelle, 1913, p. 364). No pre-1890 French printing is cited there, though Ellis’s 1890 “Lacassagne has well said” shows the line was already in circulation.

The name slips. Wikiquote’s Goldman talk page ↗ lists “A society gets all the criminals it deserves” among unsourced quotes and flags it as a misattribution, pointing back through Goldman to Ellis and Lacassagne.
source.excerptNote: Goldman reproduces Ellis’s sentence almost exactly — her 1910 text drops the “that” and emphasises the closing clause, with a footnote reading simply “THE CRIMINAL.” The popular modern form, “A society gets all the criminals it deserves,” matches neither text.

sourceLink.text: Havelock Ellis, The Criminal (1890), at Project Gutenberg

source.rightsNote: Both documented texts are comfortably pre-1931 and free of US copyright: Havelock Ellis’s The Criminal was published in 1890, and Emma Goldman’s Anarchism and Other Essays in 1910 — each is served in full by Project Gutenberg (Ellis #44500 ↗, Goldman #2162 ↗). Ellis’s English wording of Lacassagne is itself from 1890, so that text is public domain too. Note that the popular eight-word variant is a later paraphrase of that public-domain text rather than a passage from any identified work.

author.name: Alexandre Lacassagne
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Who was Alexandre Lacassagne?
author.metaLine: 1843–1924 · French forensic physician & founder of the Lyon school of criminology
author.bio: Alexandre Lacassagne was a French forensic physician who held the chair of legal medicine at Lyon and founded the journal Archives d’anthropologie criminelle. His Lyon school was the main rival to Cesare Lombroso’s Italian school: where Lombroso read criminality off the body as an inborn type, Lacassagne insisted the decisive factor was the social environment. He argued the point in portable aphorisms — the social milieu as a culture medium, the criminal as the microbe — and those aphorisms travelled far further than the theory behind them.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit went wrong
misattribution.intro: This is a quotation-marks failure rather than an invention. Goldman quoted the line accurately and named her source; the internet kept her name and discarded her citation.

items.why: Quote aggregators list “Every society has the criminals it deserves” under her name — see Goodreads ↗. In her own text she introduces it as something Ellis quotes from Lacassagne and footnotes it “THE CRIMINAL,” as the Project Gutenberg edition ↗ shows.

Kennedy wrote “In the words of the old saying, every society gets the kind of criminal it deserves” in The Pursuit of Justice (1964), per Wikiquote ↗. He signposted it as inherited; the signpost is usually dropped.

The documented English is “every society has the criminals that it deserves” (Ellis, 1890) and “every society has the criminals it deserves” (Goldman, 1910). Wikiquote ↗ lists the “gets all” form among Goldman quotes nobody has been able to source.

misattribution.truthLine: Lacassagne coined it, Havelock Ellis translated it in 1890 ↗, and Emma Goldman quoted Ellis in 1910 — correctly, with a footnote she is no longer given credit for.

context.heading: Why the sentence exists
lead: The line is a shot fired in a real argument. In the 1880s and 1890s European criminology split into two camps: Cesare Lombroso’s Italian school, which held that criminals were a distinct biological type identifiable by skull and face, and Lacassagne’s Lyon school, which held that the decisive variable was the world a person lived in. Lacassagne needed a sentence that made the second position unforgettable, and he built one out of laboratory imagery: the social environment is the culture medium, the criminal is the microbe, and a microbe does nothing at all until it lands in a broth that lets it ferment.

Havelock Ellis carried the aphorism into English in The Criminal (1890), the first comprehensive English account of criminal anthropology. Two decades on, Emma Goldman reached for exactly that passage when she wanted authority for the claim that American prisons were manufacturing the crime they punished — and because her essay was reprinted far more often than Ellis’s textbook, her page became the place most readers met the line.
detailsBody: Ellis’s 1890 English is “every society has the criminals that it deserves.” Goldman’s 1910 text drops the “that”: “every society has the criminals it deserves.” The version that now circulates on quote sites — “A society gets all the criminals it deserves” — swaps “has” for “gets,” adds “all,” and drops “every.” No printed source we could locate carries that combination.

The aphorism kept moving. Robert F. Kennedy used a further variant in The Pursuit of Justice (1964) — “In the words of the old saying, every society gets the kind of criminal it deserves” — and was careful to flag it as a saying he had inherited rather than coined. He is now widely quoted as its author too.
context.pull: “The social environment … is the cultivation medium of criminality; the criminal is the microbe.” — Lacassagne, in Ellis’s 1890 rendering

sourcesVerified.claim: Project Gutenberg hosts Havelock Ellis's The Criminal as ebook 44500.

Ellis's The Criminal, chapter I 'Introduction', reads: 'The social environment,' Lacassagne has well said, 'is the cultivation medium of criminality; the criminal is the microbe, an element which only becomes important when it finds the medium which causes it to ferment: every society has the criminals that it deserves.' The title page reads Scribner & Welford, New York, 1890, in the Contemporary Science Series edited by Havelock Ellis.
Project Gutenberg hosts Emma Goldman's Anarchism and Other Essays as ebook 2162.

Goldman's Anarchism and Other Essays contains, in 'Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure', the passage crediting Havelock Ellis quoting Quetelet and Lacassagne and ending 'EVERY SOCIETY HAS THE CRIMINALS IT DESERVES.'[4], with footnote [4] reading 'THE CRIMINAL.' The preface is dated 'New York, December, 1910.'

Wikiquote's Talk:Emma Goldman page lists 'A society gets all the criminals it deserves.' under unsourced quotes with the note: Misattribution — in Anarchism and Other Essays (1917 edition), 'Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure', Goldman cites Havelock Ellis, The Criminal (1890), as quoting Alexandre Lacassagne.

The main Wikiquote Emma Goldman article contains no quote matching 'criminals it deserves' in any of its sourced sections; its only Disputed entry concerns 'If voting changed anything, it would be made illegal.'

Alexandre Lacassagne (17 August 1843 – 24 September 1924) was a French physician and criminologist, founder of the Lacassagne school of criminology at Lyon, main rival to Lombroso's Italian school; the article records the aphorism « la justice flétrit, la prison corrompt et la société a les criminels qu'elle mérite » and a 1913 restatement of his thesis.

Marxists Internet Archive hosts Goldman's 'Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure', headed 'First published: Emma Goldman, Anarchism and Other Essays (Third revised edition, New York: Mother Earth Publishing Association, 1917)', containing the Ellis/Lacassagne passage ending 'every society has the criminals it deserves.'

Marc Renneville's Criminocorpus article reproduces Lacassagne's aphorisms in French, including « la justice flétrit, la prison corrompt et la société a les criminels qu'elle mérite » and « le milieu social est le bouillon de culture de la criminalité; le microbe, c'est le criminel… ».

Wikiquote's sourced Robert F. Kennedy page records: 'In the words of the old saying, every society gets the kind of criminal it deserves. What is equally true is that every community gets the kind of law enforcement it insists on.' — The Pursuit of Justice, pt. 3 (1964), with Lacassagne noted as the original attribution.
Goodreads attributes 'Every society has the criminals it deserves.' to Emma Goldman.
Anarchism and Other Essays by Emma Goldman was first published in 1910 by the Mother Earth Publishing Association and includes the essay 'Prisons: A Social Crime and Failure'.
The Criminal is a book by Havelock Ellis published in 1890 by Walter Scott Publishing Co. in the Contemporary Science Series.
